memory-hierarchy-001.question: Which is the best example of temporal locality?
choices: Reading each element of an array once, from start to end
Updating the same sum variable many times inside a loop
Reading data at a random address only once each time
memory-hierarchy-001.explanation: Temporal locality is the tendency to reuse data soon after using it, and a variable read and written repeatedly inside a loop is the classic example. Such data is reused while still in the cache or registers, so accesses are fast. Reading an array from start to end is an example of spatial locality, using nearby addresses in succession, which is a different property. Reading random addresses once each has almost no locality of either kind.
choiceNotes: Reading in order from the start is an example of spatial locality.
Correct. Using the same variable many times in a short span is temporal locality.
Reading random addresses once each has almost no locality.

memory-hierarchy-002.question: Scanning the 2D C array a[i][j] with j in the inner loop, as above, tends to be faster than with i in the inner loop. Why?
choices: The array is stored row-major, so consecutive addresses are read in order and each cache line is fully used
The compiler removes the additions inside the loop altogether and skips the computation entirely at run time
With j inside, the TLB is never consulted, so translating virtual addresses to physical addresses is no longer needed
memory-hierarchy-002.explanation: C stores 2D arrays in row-major order, so a[i][0], a[i][1] and so on are adjacent in memory. With j in the inner loop, consecutive addresses are read in order, so the rest of each cache line (64 bytes on most CPUs) fetched on a miss is used right away. With i inside, accesses jump a whole row apart, and lines tend to be evicted after only a small part has been used. The TLB is still used, and address translation is not eliminated.
choiceNotes: Correct. Reading consecutive addresses uses the whole of each fetched line.
The addition is not skipped; both orders perform the same computation.
The TLB is still used and addresses are still translated.

memory-hierarchy-003.question: For a direct-mapped cache with 32-bit addresses, 32 KB capacity and 64-byte lines, how many tag bits are there?
choices: 15 bits
19 bits
17 bits
memory-hierarchy-003.explanation: A 64-byte line = 2⁶, so the offset is 6 bits. The number of lines is 32 KB ÷ 64 B = 32,768 ÷ 64 = 512 = 2⁹, and in a direct-mapped cache each line is its own set, so the index is 9 bits. The rest is the tag: 32 − 9 − 6 = 17 bits. 19 bits would apply to a 4-way set-associative cache, where the index shrinks by 2 bits, not to a direct-mapped one.
choiceNotes: 15 bits results from mistaking the index for 11 bits.
19 bits applies if it were 4-way, with a quarter as many sets.
Correct. 32 − 9 (index) − 6 (offset) = 17 bits.

memory-hierarchy-004.question: How many sets does a 4-way set-associative cache with 32-bit addresses, 32 KB capacity and 64-byte lines have?
memory-hierarchy-004.explanation: The number of lines is 32 KB ÷ 64 B = 512. A 4-way cache holds four lines per set, so there are 512 ÷ 4 = 128 = 2⁷ sets, giving a 7-bit index and a 32 − 7 − 6 = 19-bit tag. 512 is the line count itself, which equals the set count only when direct-mapped. Raising associativity reduces the number of sets, which adds tag bits and comparators. 32 comes from dividing the 128 sets by the four ways a second time.
choiceNotes: Correct. 512 lines ÷ 4 ways = 128 sets.
512 is the line count, the set count for a direct-mapped cache.
32 is not the set count but the result of a wrong division.

memory-hierarchy-005.question: In a fully associative cache, how many address bits are used for the index (the part that selects a set)?
choices: 6 bits, determined by the line size
As many bits as there are lines
0 bits
memory-hierarchy-005.explanation: In a fully associative cache any data can go anywhere, so the whole cache is a single set. No set needs to be selected, so the index is 0 bits; the address splits into just offset and tag, and every access compares against all tags. That requires many comparators, so it does not suit large caches and is used for small structures such as TLBs. The line size determines the offset width, not the index.
choiceNotes: The line size determines the number of offset bits.
Index bits scaled to the line count apply to direct-mapped caches.
Correct. With only one set, no index is needed.

memory-hierarchy-006.question: With an L1 hit time of 1 ns and miss rate of 5%, an L2 hit time of 10 ns and local miss rate of 20%, and main memory access time of 100 ns, what is the average memory access time?
choices: 2.0 ns
2.5 ns
6.0 ns
memory-hierarchy-006.explanation: The L1 miss penalty is the L2 average access time, 10 + 0.2 × 100 = 30 ns. The average memory access time is therefore 1 + 0.05 × 30 = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 ns. 2.0 ns forgets the 10 ns L2 hit time, computing 1 + 0.05 × (0.2 × 100). 6.0 ns multiplies the 100 ns memory time directly by the L1 miss rate, ignoring the L2.
choiceNotes: 2.0 ns forgets to add the L2 hit time.
6.0 ns ignores the L2 and multiplies by the memory time.

memory-hierarchy-007.question: In a direct-mapped cache, elements of two arrays map to the same cache location and evict each other on every alternating access. How is this miss classified?
choices: Compulsory miss
Capacity miss
Conflict miss
memory-hierarchy-007.explanation: Misses where two pieces of data fight over the same set and evict each other, even though the cache as a whole has room, are conflict misses. Raising associativity so a set can hold both, or offsetting one array so it maps to different sets, reduces them. Capacity misses arise because the working set exceeds the whole cache and persist even with full associativity. Compulsory misses happen on first access and do not describe repeated accesses.
choiceNotes: Compulsory misses occur only on the first access.
Capacity misses occur when the whole cache is too small.
Correct. It is a conflict miss from competing for the same set.

memory-hierarchy-008.question: Which method is effective at reducing the cache misses that occur when a program accesses data for the first time?
choices: Fetching it in advance with prefetching
Doubling the cache's associativity (number of ways)
Doubling only the cache's capacity
memory-hierarchy-008.explanation: Compulsory misses on first access happen because the data has never been in the cache, so more capacity or associativity does not reduce them. Prefetching data before it is needed, or using larger lines to bring in neighboring data, does. Higher associativity reduces conflict misses from competing for the same set, and more capacity reduces capacity misses from an overflowing working set.
choiceNotes: Correct. Fetching not-yet-loaded data in advance is effective.
Higher associativity reduces conflict misses.
More capacity reduces capacity misses.

memory-hierarchy-009.question: Which misses are not reduced even by making a cache fully associative?
choices: Misses caused by two blocks competing for the same set and repeatedly evicting each other
Misses caused by the data used exceeding the cache capacity
Misses caused by uneven placement in a direct-mapped layout
memory-hierarchy-009.explanation: In a fully associative cache any data can go anywhere, so conflict misses from competing for a set disappear. But if the data a program repeatedly uses (its working set) is larger than the whole cache, it cannot fit wherever it is placed, and evictions occur. These are capacity misses, which require a larger cache or a smaller reuse footprint through techniques such as loop blocking. Uneven placement and set competition both cause conflict misses.
choiceNotes: Set competition causes conflict misses, which full associativity eliminates.
Correct. Capacity misses from an overflowing working set remain.
Misses from uneven placement are also conflict misses.

memory-hierarchy-010.question: What is the effect of increasing a cache's line size?
choices: Compulsory misses increase and the miss penalty decreases
The miss rate keeps falling monotonically for every program
Spatial locality is better exploited, but the miss penalty grows
memory-hierarchy-010.explanation: Larger lines bring in more neighboring data per miss, so workloads with spatial locality see fewer compulsory misses. On the other hand, each miss transfers more data, increasing the miss penalty, and at the same capacity there are fewer lines, raising conflict misses and loads of unused data. Lines that are too large therefore increase the miss rate rather than lowering it indefinitely. Saying compulsory misses increase gets it backwards.
choiceNotes: Compulsory misses actually decrease, and the miss penalty increases.
Lines that are too large reduce the line count and raise the miss rate.
Correct. Locality is exploited, but the miss penalty rises.

memory-hierarchy-011.question: What is the main purpose of a write buffer in a write-through cache?
choices: To let the CPU continue without waiting for writes to main memory to complete
To keep the data in the cache newer than in main memory
To always fetch the line from main memory into the cache first on a write miss, then write it
memory-hierarchy-011.explanation: A write-through cache also writes to main memory on every store, so waiting for each write to finish would stall the CPU constantly. A write buffer holds writes temporarily, letting the CPU move on immediately while the buffer drains to memory in the background. Keeping the cache newer than memory characterizes write-back caches; with write-through the two stay consistent. Whether to load a line on a write miss is the write-allocate decision, separate from the write buffer.
choiceNotes: Correct. It holds writes temporarily so the CPU need not wait.
The cache becomes newer than memory under write-back.
Loading on a miss is the write-allocate decision.

memory-hierarchy-012.question: In a write-back cache, what is the role of the dirty bit attached to each line?
choices: It shows whether the line's data is valid and can be read
It shows the line was modified and differs from memory
It shows the time the line was last accessed
memory-hierarchy-012.explanation: A write-back cache completes writes in the cache alone, so some lines end up newer than main memory. The dirty bit marks such modified lines so that only dirty lines need to be written back on eviction; clean lines can simply be discarded, avoiding wasted writes. Validity is indicated by the valid bit, and access order is tracked by separate replacement information such as LRU state.
choiceNotes: Validity is indicated by the valid bit.
Correct. It marks the line as modified, deciding whether it is written back on eviction.
Access order is separate information used by the replacement policy.

memory-hierarchy-013.question: Which policy, on a write miss, writes directly to the lower level without loading the line into the cache?
choices: Write-allocate
Write-back
No-write-allocate
memory-hierarchy-013.explanation: Writing straight to the lower level on a write miss without loading the line is no-write-allocate, commonly paired with write-through. It avoids useless fetches for data that is written once and not read back. Write-allocate instead loads the line and then writes it, which pays off when written data is soon reused, so it is commonly paired with write-back. Write-back governs when hits are propagated to memory, a separate axis from whether a miss loads the line.
choiceNotes: Write-allocate loads the line and then writes it.
Write-back concerns when writes reach memory, separate from the miss decision.
Correct. It writes to the lower level without loading the line.

memory-hierarchy-014.question: A fully associative cache holding 2 lines with LRU replacement starts empty. If blocks are referenced in the order A, B, A, C, B, A, how many misses occur?
memory-hierarchy-014.explanation: Step by step: A (miss, [A]), B (miss, [A,B]), A (hit, A becomes most recent), C (miss, evicts least recent B, [A,C]), B (miss, evicts least recent A, [C,B]), A (miss, evicts least recent C, [B,A]), for 5 misses. Counting 4 comes from wrongly evicting A when C arrives; under LRU, the hit on A made it the most recent. 6 overlooks the hit on the third reference.
choiceNotes: 4 results from evicting the wrong block.
Correct. Only the third reference (A) hits, giving 5 misses.
6 overlooks the hit on the third reference to A.

memory-hierarchy-015.question: For which access pattern is hardware prefetching especially effective?
choices: Reading an array in order at a fixed interval (stride)
Following a linked list one element at a time from the head
Looking up a hash table with random keys
memory-hierarchy-015.explanation: A hardware prefetcher detects regularity in recent addresses, such as sequential or constant-stride patterns, predicts upcoming addresses and loads them ahead of time. Reading an array at a fixed stride is easy to predict, so the benefit is large. In a linked list the next element's address is unknown until the current one is read, so there is no pattern to predict. Random-key hash lookups also lack address regularity, so prefetching helps little.
choiceNotes: Correct. Regular strides are easy to predict, so the benefit is large.
The next address is unknown until the current element is read, so it cannot be predicted.
Addresses have no regularity, so the benefit is small.

memory-hierarchy-016.question: When inserting software prefetch instructions, which statement about how far ahead to fetch (the prefetch distance) is correct?
choices: Shorter is better; inserting it just before the next element is read is optimal
Longer is better; fetching all the data the loop will use at the very start is optimal
Neither too short nor too long; it is chosen from the miss latency and the time per iteration
memory-hierarchy-016.explanation: A prefetch is useless unless the data arrives from memory before it is needed. If the distance is too short, the data arrives late; if too long, fetched data may be evicted before use or pollute the cache. A rule of thumb is to fetch ahead by the miss penalty divided by the time per loop iteration. Prefetching just before use cannot hide latency, and fetching everything up front does not fit in the cache.
choiceNotes: Just before use, the fetch cannot complete in time and latency is not hidden.
Fetching everything first gets data evicted before it is used.
Correct. Choose a distance that arrives in time yet is not evicted, from the miss latency and iteration time.

memory-hierarchy-017.question: In the loop above, an int is 4 bytes, a cache line is 64 bytes, and the array is not cached and starts on a line boundary. Without prefetching, what is the miss rate for reading the array?
memory-hierarchy-017.explanation: A 64-byte line holds 64 ÷ 4 = 16 ints. Reading in order misses once on the first element of each line and hits on the remaining 15, so the miss rate is 1 ÷ 16 = 6.25%. For 1,024 elements that is 1,024 ÷ 16 = 64 misses. 12.5% would result from thinking only eight elements fit in a line. 100% occurs only when one element per line is used, such as reading every 16th element (every 64 bytes).
choiceNotes: 12.5% results from assuming eight elements per line.
Correct. One miss every 16 elements gives 1/16 = 6.25%.
100% occurs with strided access that uses one element per line.

memory-hierarchy-018.question: What is the main purpose of loop blocking (tiling), used for example in matrix multiplication?
choices: To compute in small cache-sized blocks and increase data reuse
To reduce the number of iterations and hence the branch instructions executed at the end of each iteration
To halve total memory usage without changing the order of computation
memory-hierarchy-018.explanation: Computing a large matrix product directly evicts elements before they are reused, forcing repeated reloads from main memory. Loop blocking splits the matrices into small blocks that fit in the cache and finishes the work within each block, reusing loaded data many times and sharply reducing capacity misses. Reducing branches is the goal of loop unrolling, and total memory usage does not change.
choiceNotes: Correct. Computing in cache-sized units increases data reuse.
Reducing branches is the goal of loop unrolling.
The order of computation changes, and total memory usage stays the same.

memory-hierarchy-019.question: For a loop that sums only the x coordinates as above, why does converting to a structure of arrays (a separate array per field) tend to be faster?
choices: As an array of structures, the compiler cannot generate instructions that read only the x field
Separate arrays make the floating-point computation more precise
The x values are contiguous, so fetched lines carry no unneeded fields
memory-hierarchy-019.explanation: In an array of structures (AoS), x, y, z and mass form a 16-byte group, so even a loop reading only x wastes three quarters of each 64-byte line. With a structure of arrays (SoA), the x values are contiguous, every fetched line is fully used, and memory traffic drops to about a quarter. It also makes SIMD vectorization easier. Compilers can read x from AoS, and changing the layout does not change numerical precision.
choiceNotes: Compilers can read x from an AoS layout just fine.
Changing the data layout does not change precision.
Correct. Only the needed x values are contiguous, so lines are used without waste.

memory-hierarchy-020.question: What is the main advantage of splitting the L1 cache into an instruction cache (I-cache) and a data cache (D-cache)?
choices: Instructions and data no longer collide even at the same address, so capacity seems doubled
Instruction fetch and data reads or writes can proceed in parallel in the same clock cycle
Since instructions are not modified, the D-cache can be eliminated
memory-hierarchy-020.explanation: In a pipeline, an instruction is fetched every cycle while another instruction reads or writes data. Splitting L1 into instruction and data caches lets these two accesses proceed in parallel without contending for a single cache port, and each can be organized to suit its own behavior. Capacity is not doubled; the total is divided between them. Data accesses are always needed, so the D-cache cannot be dropped. L2 and beyond are usually unified.
choiceNotes: The total capacity is merely divided; it is not doubled.
Correct. Instruction fetch and data access can proceed in parallel.
Data accesses are required, so the D-cache cannot be eliminated.

memory-hierarchy-021.question: In a system with 4 KB pages and 64-byte lines, an L1 cache is to be virtually indexed and physically tagged (VIPT) with the index and offset taken only from page-offset bits. If it is 8-way set-associative, what is its maximum capacity?
choices: 32 KB
4 KB
256 KB
memory-hierarchy-021.explanation: Addresses within a 4 KB = 2¹² page use 12 bits, which are identical in virtual and physical addresses. Keeping index plus offset within 12 bits limits each way to 2¹² = 4 KB. With 8 ways, the cache can be up to 4 KB × 8 = 32 KB. 4 KB gives only the capacity of one way. At 256 KB the index would include page-number bits, letting the same physical address land in different sets.
choiceNotes: Correct. 4 KB per way × 8 ways = 32 KB.
4 KB is the capacity of a single way.
At 256 KB the index no longer fits within the page offset.

memory-hierarchy-022.question: Why are L1 caches often virtually indexed and physically tagged (VIPT)?
choices: Physical addresses are not needed, so the TLB can be omitted
Hits are judged only by virtual addresses, so the cache can be flushed on every process switch
The cache set can be read in parallel while the TLB translates the address
memory-hierarchy-022.explanation: A VIPT cache selects the set with page-offset bits that need no translation, so reading the set can start at the same time as the TLB produces the physical address. The final comparison uses the physical tag, so different processes using the same virtual address are not confused. The TLB is required to obtain the physical tag and cannot be omitted. Needing to flush the cache on every process switch is a drawback of virtually tagged designs.
choiceNotes: The TLB is needed to compare physical tags.
Flushing on every switch is a drawback of virtually tagged caches.
Correct. Translation and set lookup proceed in parallel.

memory-hierarchy-023.question: With a cache hit time of 2 cycles, a miss rate of 4% and a miss penalty of 150 cycles, what is the average memory access time in cycles?
choices: 8 cycles
6 cycles
152 cycles
memory-hierarchy-023.explanation: Average memory access time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty = 2 + 0.04 × 150 = 2 + 6 = 8 cycles. The hit time applies to every access, and the miss penalty is added only on misses. 6 cycles omits the hit time, counting only the misses. 152 cycles is the time for a single access that misses, not the average. Even a 4% miss rate quadruples the average.
choiceNotes: Correct. 2 + 0.04 × 150 = 8 cycles.
6 cycles forgets to add the hit time.
152 cycles is the time for one access that misses.

memory-hierarchy-024.question: A processor has an average CPI of 1.0 with a perfect cache. Each instruction makes 1.3 memory accesses on average, with a 2% miss rate and a 100-cycle miss penalty. What is the actual average CPI?
memory-hierarchy-024.explanation: Memory stall cycles per instruction are 1.3 accesses × 0.02 × 100 cycles = 2.6 cycles. Adding them to the ideal CPI gives 1.0 + 2.6 = 3.6, so performance falls to 1/3.6 of ideal. 3.0 wrongly assumes one access per instruction (1.0 + 1 × 0.02 × 100). 1.3 is the number of accesses per instruction, not the CPI. Even a small miss rate badly hurts performance when the miss penalty is large.
choiceNotes: 3.0 wrongly assumes one access per instruction.
1.3 is the number of accesses per instruction.

memory-hierarchy-025.question: What is the main advantage of a non-blocking cache, which accepts other accesses while a miss is being serviced?
choices: It reduces the number of cache misses compared with a blocking cache
Missed data can be read from main memory faster
Miss latencies overlap, and hits proceed meanwhile
memory-hierarchy-025.explanation: In a blocking cache, every subsequent access waits until a miss is serviced. A non-blocking cache keeps miss information in dedicated registers (MSHRs), so it can return hits during a miss and send other misses to memory at the same time. This overlaps and hides latency, but the number of misses is unchanged, as is the time to read one miss from memory. It pays off in combination with out-of-order execution.
choiceNotes: The miss count is unchanged; the benefit is overlapping latency.
The time to read from main memory itself does not change.
Correct. Miss latencies overlap, and hits are serviced meanwhile.

memory-hierarchy-026.question: If the L1 miss rate (as a fraction of all accesses) is 4% and the L2 global miss rate (the fraction of all accesses that also miss in L2) is 1%, what is the L2 local miss rate?
memory-hierarchy-026.explanation: The local miss rate is the fraction of accesses reaching a cache that miss there. L2 receives the 4% of all accesses that miss in L1, and 1% of all accesses miss in L2 as well, so the local miss rate is 1 ÷ 4 = 25%. The high local rate does not mean L2 is ineffective; L2 only sees the low-locality accesses L1 could not capture. 1% is the global miss rate relative to all accesses, and 4% is the L1 miss rate.
choiceNotes: Correct. 1% out of the 4% reaching L2 gives 25%.
4% is the L1 miss rate.
1% is the global miss rate relative to all accesses.

memory-hierarchy-027.question: With 64 TLB entries and a 4 KB page size, how much memory can be accessed without TLB misses (the TLB reach)?
choices: 64 KB
256 KB
4 MB
memory-hierarchy-027.explanation: Each TLB entry holds the translation for one page, so TLB reach = entries × page size = 64 × 4 KB = 256 KB. Programs that frequently touch a wider range suffer more TLB misses. With 2 MB huge pages, the same 64 entries reach 64 × 2 MB = 128 MB. 64 KB results from mistaking the page size for 1 KB, and 4 MB from mistaking it for 64 KB.
choiceNotes: 64 KB results from assuming a 1 KB page.
Correct. 64 entries × 4 KB = 256 KB.
4 MB results from assuming a 64 KB page.

memory-hierarchy-028.question: Which pair correctly states the main advantage and drawback of using large pages (huge pages)?
choices: Advantage: lower cache miss rate. Drawback: more TLB misses
Advantage: page faults disappear. Drawback: more disk space is used
Advantage: fewer TLB misses. Drawback: more internal fragmentation
memory-hierarchy-028.explanation: Larger pages let one TLB entry translate a wide range, sharply reducing TLB misses for programs with large data. On the other hand, even small amounts of data are allocated in large page units, increasing unused space (internal fragmentation) and making allocation less flexible. TLB misses decrease rather than increase, and the cache miss rate does not depend directly on page size. Page faults do not disappear either.
choiceNotes: TLB misses actually decrease, and the cache miss rate is not directly affected.
Page faults do not disappear.
Correct. TLB misses fall, but internal fragmentation grows.

memory-hierarchy-029.question: When each row of a 2D array is 4,096 bytes (a power of two), walking down a column can cause many misses even though the cache has spare capacity. Which countermeasure is effective?
choices: Padding each row so its size is not a power of two
Changing the element type to a different type of the same size
Relocating the whole array so it starts on a large power-of-two address boundary
memory-hierarchy-029.explanation: With rows exactly 4096 bytes long, elements down a column are spaced by multiples of 4096, so the index bits within the low 12 address bits are identical and the elements crowd into a few sets (all into the same set in an L1 cache with 4 KB or less per way). When more rows than the associativity map to one set, conflict misses occur even with capacity to spare. Padding each row by about one line shifts the set for each element and spreads them out. Aligning to a power of two leaves the problem intact, and a same-sized type changes nothing.
choiceNotes: Correct. Shifting the row size spreads elements across different sets.
A type of the same size leaves the addresses unchanged.
Aligning to a power of two leaves the concentration in one set.

memory-hierarchy-030.question: Roughly how many times longer is a main-memory DRAM access than an L1 cache hit (for typical PC or server CPUs)?
choices: 2 to 3 times
Tens to about a hundred times
More than 100,000 times
memory-hierarchy-030.explanation: An L1 hit takes a few cycles (around 1 ns), while a DRAM access takes tens to about 100 ns, a difference of tens to a hundred times. For a CPU running at several GHz that means waiting hundreds of cycles, which is why cache hierarchies and prefetching are essential to performance. If the gap were only 2 to 3 times, caches would matter far less. More than 100,000 times is closer to the gap with SSDs or hard disks, not DRAM.
choiceNotes: The gap is far larger than 2 to 3 times.
Correct. Tens to a hundred times, equal to hundreds of CPU cycles.
More than 100,000 times is closer to the gap with storage.

memory-hierarchy-031.question: What is the role of the valid bit attached to each cache line?
choices: It shows whether the line has been modified
It shows the order in which the line will be evicted
It shows if real data is present
memory-hierarchy-031.explanation: Right after power-up or after a line is invalidated, cache contents are meaningless. A line whose valid bit is 0 is not counted as a hit even if its tag happens to match; the bit is set to 1 when correct data is loaded. This prevents empty lines from being mistaken for hits. Modification is shown by the dirty bit used in write-back caches, and eviction order is tracked by replacement information such as LRU state.
choiceNotes: Modification is shown by the dirty bit.
Eviction order is separate replacement-policy information.
Correct. It shows whether real data is present, preventing false hits on empty lines.

memory-hierarchy-032.question: What is the main effect of a victim cache, a small fully associative buffer that temporarily holds lines evicted from the L1 cache?
choices: Lines reused right after eviction can be recovered quickly, reducing the cost of conflict misses
It reduces capacity misses as much as enlarging the L1 cache would
It eliminates compulsory misses and makes prefetching unnecessary
memory-hierarchy-032.explanation: In direct-mapped and similar caches, data competing for the same set evicts each other, and a just-evicted line is often needed again soon. A victim cache holds a few to a dozen or so evicted lines, so an L1 miss that finds the line there is served faster than from the next level. Being small, it does little for capacity misses, and it cannot help compulsory misses for data never loaded.
choiceNotes: Correct. It rescues reuse right after eviction, cutting the cost of conflict misses.
It holds only a handful of lines, so its effect on capacity misses is small.
It cannot help data that was never loaded.

memory-hierarchy-033.question: In a multilevel cache with an L2 below the L1, what is the L2's main role?
choices: To eliminate L1 misses altogether by having a faster hit time than the L1
Larger and slower than L1, it reduces the L1 miss penalty
To always hold all of the program's data in place of main memory
memory-hierarchy-033.explanation: L1 is built small for speed, so some misses are inevitable. L2 is larger with a longer hit time but still much faster than main memory, so it catches most L1 misses and cuts the L1 miss penalty well below a trip to memory. It is not faster than L1 and cannot eliminate L1 misses. Its capacity is far smaller than main memory, so it cannot hold all data.
choiceNotes: L2 is slower than L1 and cannot eliminate L1 misses.
Correct. It absorbs most L1 misses, reducing the miss penalty.
Its capacity is far smaller than main memory, so not all data fits.

memory-hierarchy-034.question: Which describes an inclusive cache, where a lower level (such as L2) contains everything in the upper level (L1)?
choices: Upper and lower levels never hold the same data, so total capacity is used most efficiently
The lower cache must always be smaller than the upper one
Coherence is easier to manage, but data is duplicated
memory-hierarchy-034.explanation: In an inclusive design, anything in L1 is guaranteed to be in L2, so snoops from other cores can be answered by checking L2 alone, without probing L1. The cost is duplicated data, leaving effective capacity at roughly the L2 size. Not duplicating data is the exclusive design, which uses total capacity efficiently. Lower-level caches are normally larger than upper ones.
choiceNotes: Avoiding duplication describes an exclusive cache.
Lower-level caches are normally larger than upper ones.
Correct. Coherence is easier, but data is duplicated.

memory-hierarchy-035.question: What changes when a cache is switched from direct-mapped to set-associative?
choices: Conflict misses decrease, but tag comparison and way selection tend to lengthen hit time
Conflict misses increase, but simpler circuits shorten hit time
Neither miss rate nor hit time changes at all, regardless of associativity
memory-hierarchy-035.explanation: A set-associative cache has several ways per set, so multiple blocks mapping to the same set can coexist, reducing conflict misses compared with a direct-mapped cache. The cost is circuitry that compares several tags in parallel and selects the matching way, which tends to increase hit time and power. More conflict misses and simpler circuits describe the direct-mapped side. Both miss rate and hit time change with associativity.
choiceNotes: Correct. Conflict misses drop, but hit time tends to increase.
This is reversed and describes a direct-mapped cache.
Miss rate and hit time both change with associativity.

memory-hierarchy-036.question: In an 8-way set-associative cache, how many tags are compared in parallel on each access?
choices: As many as there are lines in the whole cache
memory-hierarchy-036.explanation: A set-associative cache first selects one set with the index bits, then compares the tags of every way in that set in parallel. With 8 ways a set holds 8 lines, so 8 tags are compared, requiring 8 comparators. Comparing against every line in the cache is fully associative, and comparing just one is direct-mapped. More ways mean more comparators and power, which is why L1 associativity is often kept modest.
choiceNotes: Comparing against every line is fully associative.
Correct. It compares the tags of the 8 ways in the selected set.
Comparing only one tag is direct-mapped.

memory-hierarchy-037.question: In a cache with 64-byte lines and 64 sets, which set holds the data at address 0x1234?
memory-hierarchy-037.explanation: The offset is the low 6 bits (64 = 2⁶), and the index is the next 6 bits (64 sets = 2⁶). 0x1234 = 4,660, and 4,660 ÷ 64 = 72 remainder 52, so the line number is 72. The set number is the line number modulo the set count: 72 mod 64 = 8. 52 is the remainder, the position within the line (offset). 4 is merely the last hexadecimal digit of the address and has nothing to do with the set.
choiceNotes: 4 is just the last hex digit and unrelated to the set.
52 is the position within the line (offset).
Correct. Line number 72 modulo 64 gives 8.

memory-hierarchy-038.question: For code that writes to the same line many times, why is a write-back cache more advantageous than write-through?
choices: Writes complete within the cache, and memory is written only once when the line is evicted
Memory is updated on every write, so no work is needed at eviction
Cache and memory always match, so no coherence management is needed
memory-hierarchy-038.explanation: A write-back cache absorbs repeated writes to the same line within the cache and writes the dirty line back just once on eviction, greatly reducing memory traffic and power. Updating memory on every write is the write-through behavior, which generates traffic each time the line is written. Cache and memory always matching is also write-through; with write-back they differ for a while.
choiceNotes: Correct. Many writes collapse into one write-back at eviction.
Updating memory on every write is write-through.
Always matching is write-through; with write-back they can differ.

memory-hierarchy-039.question: In contrast to LRU, which evicts the least recently used block, optimal replacement (OPT) evicts the block that will not be used for the longest time. Which statement about OPT is correct?
choices: It is the most common replacement policy, widely used in real caches
It cannot be built but gives a lower bound on misses
It produces exactly the same number of misses as LRU for every access sequence
memory-hierarchy-039.explanation: Optimal replacement (Bélády's OPT) assumes the future access order is known and evicts the block whose next use is furthest away, giving the theoretical minimum number of misses. Real hardware cannot see the future, so it cannot be implemented; instead it is applied to recorded access traces to evaluate how close policies such as LRU come to optimal. It evicts different blocks than LRU, so miss counts generally differ.
choiceNotes: It requires knowing the future, so real caches cannot use it.
Correct. It cannot be built but provides a lower bound on misses.
It evicts different blocks, so miss counts generally differ.

memory-hierarchy-040.question: What generally happens to hit time as cache capacity increases, and why?
choices: It shortens, because more data inside means less time searching
It stays the same, because hit time depends only on line size
It tends to lengthen, as wiring and selection logic grow
memory-hierarchy-040.explanation: A larger cache lowers the miss rate, but the memory array grows, wires lengthen, and the index decoding and output selection circuits get bigger, so hit time tends to increase. That is why L1 is kept small, around tens of KB, while large capacity is provided by L2 and L3 in a multilevel hierarchy. Hit time does not shorten, nor does it depend on line size alone. Capacity is set by balancing miss rate against hit time.
choiceNotes: Making it larger does not shorten the search; it lengthens it.
Hit time also depends on capacity and associativity.
Correct. Larger wiring and selection circuits tend to lengthen hit time.

memory-hierarchy-041.question: Why does traversing the linked list above tend to be much slower than reading an array with the same number of elements in order?
choices: The next element's address is unknown until the current one is read, so misses occur one after another
Linked-list elements are, by rule, never placed in the cache
The CPU's branch prediction always fails in code that uses pointers
memory-hierarchy-041.explanation: In a linked list the next element's address is known only after reading p->next. If elements are scattered in memory, each access misses, and since the next address is unknown, misses cannot overlap, so the full memory latency piles up element by element. With an array the next address can be computed, so prefetching and overlapping misses work. Linked-list elements are cached like any data, and the loop branch is predictable rather than always mispredicted.
choiceNotes: Correct. The next address is unknown, so miss latencies accumulate one by one.
Linked-list elements are cached like any other data.
The loop branch is regular, and prediction does not always fail.

memory-hierarchy-042.question: Each miss fetches a 64-byte line and memory latency is 100 ns. With only one miss outstanding at a time, read bandwidth is about 0.64 GB/s. If 10 misses can be outstanding at once, what is the bandwidth approximately (assuming no other limits)?
choices: 6.4 GB/s
memory-hierarchy-042.explanation: Bandwidth equals the amount of data in flight divided by latency (Little's law). With one miss, 64 B ÷ 100 ns = 0.64 GB/s; with 10 outstanding, 10 × 64 B ÷ 100 ns = 6.4 GB/s. Saturating memory bandwidth requires not just lower latency but memory-level parallelism, servicing many misses at once. 0.64 GB/s is the single-miss value unchanged, and 0.064 GB/s divides by 10 instead of multiplying.
choiceNotes: 0.064 GB/s divides by 10 instead of multiplying.
0.64 GB/s is the value with only one outstanding miss.
Correct. 10 × 64 B ÷ 100 ns = 6.4 GB/s.

memory-hierarchy-043.question: When writing out a large amount of data that will not be read back for a while, what is the main benefit of non-temporal stores that bypass the cache?
choices: The written data stays in the cache longer and is faster to read later
The cache is not filled with data that won't be reused
Write ordering is no longer guaranteed, making program bugs easier to find
memory-hierarchy-043.explanation: Ordinary stores with write-allocate fetch the line from memory before writing, so even write-only data costs read traffic and evicts other data that will be reused. Non-temporal stores combine writes and send them straight to memory, leaving the cache unpolluted and skipping useless fetches. The data does not stay in the cache, so reading it back soon would be slower. Changed ordering semantics are a caveat, not a benefit.
choiceNotes: The data does not stay cached, so reading it soon is actually slower.
Correct. The cache is not filled with non-reused data, and useless fetches are avoided.
Changed ordering is a caveat, not a benefit.

memory-hierarchy-044.question: If the cache hit rate is 95%, what is the miss rate?
memory-hierarchy-044.explanation: Every access is either a hit or a miss, so miss rate = 1 − hit rate = 100% − 95% = 5%. A small-looking miss rate still matters a lot when the miss penalty is large: with a 1-cycle hit time and a 100-cycle penalty, the average is 1 + 0.05 × 100 = 6 cycles, shrinking to 2 cycles at a 99% hit rate. 95% is the hit rate itself, and 0.95% confuses a fraction with a percentage.
choiceNotes: 95% is the hit rate itself.
0.95% confuses a fraction with a percentage.

memory-hierarchy-045.question: Which technique, when fetching a missed line from memory, sends the word the CPU needs first and the rest afterward?
choices: Critical word first
Write-allocate
Victim cache
memory-hierarchy-045.explanation: Waiting for the whole 64-byte line before handing over data lengthens the CPU's stall. Critical word first transfers the requested word first and passes it to the CPU immediately, filling in the rest of the line afterward, which shortens the effective miss penalty. Write-allocate concerns whether a write miss loads the line, and a victim cache is a small buffer for evicted lines; neither relates to transfer order.
choiceNotes: Correct. Sending the needed word first shortens the wait.
Write-allocate concerns how write misses are handled.
A victim cache is a buffer for evicted lines.

memory-hierarchy-046.question: Why does fusing the two loops above into one (loop fusion) tend to be faster when N is large?
choices: The multiply and add merge into one instruction, halving the computation
a[i] is used right after being written, so array a need not be reloaded from main memory
The iteration count rises from N to 2N, keeping the pipeline full
memory-hierarchy-046.explanation: With separate loops, if all of a written by the first loop does not fit in the cache, the second loop misses as it rereads a from the start. Fused, each a[i] is used in the same iteration right after it is written, so it is reused while still in cache or registers and memory traffic drops. The amount of computation is unchanged, and the iteration count falls from 2N to N.
choiceNotes: The number of operations is unchanged; computation is not halved.
Correct. Reuse right after writing avoids rereading array a.
The iteration count falls from 2N to N.

memory-hierarchy-047.question: Which pair gives the reason a large matrix transpose (b[j][i] = a[i][j]) tends to cause many cache misses, and a typical countermeasure?
choices: Reason: heavy computation. Countermeasure: switch floating point to integers
Reason: reads are strided. Countermeasure: make only the writes sequential
Reason: reads or writes are column-wise. Countermeasure: blocked transpose
memory-hierarchy-047.explanation: In a transpose, reading a row-wise means writing b column-wise, and writing b row-wise means reading a column-wise, so one side is always strided. Splitting the matrices into small cache-sized blocks and transposing within each block uses fetched lines fully before moving on, sharply reducing misses. Making only the writes sequential just moves the strided access to the reads, solving nothing. Computation is not the issue.
choiceNotes: A transpose does almost no computation, and changing types does not help.
Making one side sequential only makes the other side strided.
Correct. One side is always column-wise, so transpose block by block.

memory-hierarchy-048.question: In a typical computer's memory hierarchy, which property holds more strongly for upper levels (closer to the CPU)?
choices: Faster, but smaller in capacity and more expensive per bit
Slower, but larger in capacity and cheaper per bit
Faster, larger and cheaper per bit
memory-hierarchy-048.explanation: Storage closer to the CPU, such as registers and L1 cache, is faster but uses area-hungry circuits such as SRAM, so it costs more per bit and has less capacity. Lower levels are slower but cheaper and larger, continuing to DRAM main memory and then storage such as SSDs. If fast, large and cheap memory existed there would be no need for a hierarchy; since it does not, the hierarchy exploits locality to keep needed data in small, fast memory.
choiceNotes: Correct. Upper levels are faster but smaller and costlier per bit.
This describes lower levels, farther from the CPU.
A hierarchy is needed precisely because fast, large and cheap memory does not exist.

memory-hierarchy-049.question: Why must cache designs be compared by average memory access time rather than miss rate alone?
choices: Miss rate cannot be measured, while average memory access time is easy to measure
A lower miss rate may come with a longer hit time and a slower average
Average memory access time depends only on the miss rate, not the hit time
memory-hierarchy-049.explanation: More associativity or capacity lowers the miss rate but can lengthen the hit time. Comparing a 1-cycle hit with a 5% miss rate against a 2-cycle hit with a 4% miss rate, at a 20-cycle miss penalty, gives 1 + 0.05 × 20 = 2.0 versus 2 + 0.04 × 20 = 2.8, so the lower miss rate is slower. Average memory access time depends on hit time, miss rate and miss penalty together. Miss rates can be measured with performance counters and similar tools.
choiceNotes: Miss rates can be measured with performance counters and the like.
Correct. A better miss rate can be offset by a worse hit time.
The average depends on hit time, miss rate and miss penalty.

memory-hierarchy-050.question: Running two programs alternately on the same core can make each slower than running alone. What is the best explanation from a cache perspective?
choices: Alternating doubles the number of instructions that each of the two programs executes
Alternating reconfigures the cache to half its capacity
The other program evicts one's data, causing reloads
memory-hierarchy-050.explanation: When programs switch, the caches and TLB fill with the other program's data, so by the time a program runs again its data has been evicted. Accesses that would hit when running alone now miss, costing time to reload from main memory. The shorter the interval between switches, the larger the effect. Instruction counts are unchanged and cache capacity is not reconfigured; the slowdown comes from sharing the cache.
choiceNotes: Each program's instruction count is unchanged.
Cache capacity does not change.
Correct. The other program's data evicts one's own, increasing reload misses.
